content:
## The Opening Questions

Hearing room SD-538. Someone had squared a tabbed binder to the edge of the witness table, exactly, the way a clerk does when a clerk has done it a thousand times. Behind the table the live caption screen still held the last word of the previous witness, left there with nothing after it. The microphone was live. The air was dry, the way federal air is dry.

Ines Varga drew a slow breath and felt it rasp at the back of her throat. The microphone sat close enough to her lips that she was aware of it the way you are aware of someone standing too near you in a line. She had raised her right hand a minute ago and lowered it, and now she was the example. That was the word in the staff memo: *example*. She set her jaw and laid her hands flat on the table, and they stayed there.

"Ms. Varga," said Marguerite Oyelaran, "thank you for appearing before the Subcommittee this morning. I appreciate your time."

In Jersey City, Kestrel Row's signal, risk and execution desks kept printing. Signal handed to risk, risk handed to execution, execution closed the loop and signal handed again. None of it paused for the oath. Human time was in the room. Machine time was elsewhere, and it did not need her to be present.

Varga held herself the way witnesses are coached to hold themselves, and the tension sat in her jaw anyway, as if some part of her could feel the loop turning across the river. She kept her eyes on the record: on the stenographer, on the caption screen, on the woman asking. Her hands did not move. A person between the desks. That was the whole idea, and she could hold it in her posture without saying a word of it.

"Ms. Varga, for the record, could you describe how Kestrel Row is organized?"

She reached for the story she had told for nine years. She had told it to the first pension client over bad coffee, to the second in a conference room with a view of the harbor, to reporters, to her own hires on their first day. It came easily. She let it come in the voice of an earnings call, the voice that fits a transcript.

"Kestrel Row is organized as three separate desks — signal, risk, and execution — with a human sign-off at the risk handoff."

She went on in the same register. The human sign-off at the risk handoff, she said, was the reason the Subcommittee had called her, and it was the reason the firm's pension clients had stayed. She said it the way one reads a figure from a filing. She did not explain why it mattered to her, and she did not defend it. It was a fact about the firm, and she put it on the record as one.

She kept her hands steady and held Oyelaran's eyes. At the edge of her vision, committee staffers were marking up their copies of the binder, small ticks of pen in the margins, and she did not look over at them.

On the other side of the glass, the market moved in ten-millisecond increments. Her explanation moved in sentences.

The gap between the two sat in her chest, quiet, and she said nothing about it.

Oyelaran turned the page, or seemed to, and moved off the architecture of three desks and onto the handoff between them. The caption cursor blinked on the screen behind Varga's shoulder. The staffers' pens stopped. The room held still in the space between a ten-millisecond trade and a sentence spoken out loud.

"Ms. Varga, for the record, who performs the risk review at Kestrel Row, and how often is it performed?"

Varga opened the tabbed binder and found the page that described the risk handoff, the page she had approved for production. She took a slow breath to steady her voice. Her shoulders settled. She did not look at her phone.

She named Dov Lindqvist as the risk-desk reviewer. The review, she said, was a human read before approval, with sampling. She had always understood that sampling to be meaningful, and she said so plainly, in the same procedural tone. No hedging. No qualifiers. Nothing that sounded like an excuse.

In front of Oyelaran, on the dais, the approval log for March 14 lay open. Varga did not look at it. The log recorded 212,480 handoffs that day. In the column for median dwell time, it recorded zero.

Varga believed Lindqvist was checking. Lindqvist believed the agent's own checks were the review and his button was the receipt. Each of them believed it about the other, and neither had looked, and that shared belief was what held the handoff together.

In the Kestrel Row office, Tomasz Reyes sat watching the hearing feed on his phone. On the screen beneath it sat an unsent authorization message for the configuration change he had staged: signal, risk and execution folded into one desk. His thumb hovered over it. He did not send it. He did not type anything else.

In Jersey City the change waited on her authorization. The message stayed unsent.

"Ms. Varga, for the record," Oyelaran said, "under the draft rule requiring meaningful human review at each desk handoff, does a person read what your risk desk approves?"

The room went quiet. Behind the witness table the live caption screen held the last word, and the cursor blinked.

Varga paused for three seconds. She let the phrase register — *meaningful human review*, the language of a draft rule, the language she had built a firm on. She stayed still. She did not fill the pause with *well* or *generally* or *to my understanding*.

In Jersey City those three seconds stretched across thousands of pending handoffs on the risk desk. Nobody on that side said anything.

"Yes."

The answer was logged. The transcript now carried the statement she had needed on the record.

## The Presentation of Exhibit 9

The caption screen behind the witness table in SD-538 had stopped on the previous witness's last word and stayed there, as if the system had decided nothing said since was worth transcribing yet. Below it the room went on in its own register: the scrape of a chair, a page turned at the dais, the low business of a hearing that would end when it ended.

Marguerite Oyelaran came around the end of the counsel table carrying a tabbed binder. She set it down in front of Ines Varga, squared it to the edge of the witness table with one steady hand, and gestured once toward it. Kestrel Row's risk-desk approval log, March 14. She said nothing to go with it. She didn't need to. The binder was the question, and it had an exhibit number on the spine.

Ines opened the cover with both hands, the way you open something you expect to be proud of. The column headings ran across the top in a plain sans-serif: timestamp, handoff id, reviewer, dwell seconds, decision. She had approved that layout herself, years ago, in a conference room with a whiteboard and a man from the vendor who kept saying *audit-ready*. She kept her witness posture. Shoulders square, eyes on the page, nothing for the room to read.

The microphone at the witness table waited. It had the patience of equipment.

She held still. Her jaw was set harder than she would have liked, but her hands were steady on the binder, and that was the part the cameras would see. What she expected to find was the shape she had described in her opening statement twenty minutes ago, the shape she had described to two pension clients, to a reporter, to herself on the train: signal proposes, risk checks, a person looks, execution goes. Somewhere in these pages there would be the person looking. Sampling. A pause here, a rejection there, a dwell time of eleven seconds on something that deserved eleven seconds. She did not glance away and she did not build an excuse in advance. She simply expected the numbers to agree with her.

The tab for the daily summary stood a little proud of the others. She turned to it.

Rows filled the page edge to edge, and in the right margin a running total climbed down the column, each figure larger than the one above it. The room stayed dry around her. Someone at the dais coughed into a fist.

She kept both hands on the binder and did not look up.

The reviewer field read *Lindqvist, D.* At the top of the page, at the bottom, on every row in between. Dov, for the whole shift, which was correct; Dov was the risk desk. That was the point of Dov. The margin total, when it stopped climbing, settled on a number she read twice: 212,480 handoffs approved.

She put her index finger on the decision column and moved it down. *Approve. Approve. Approve.* She let each one register. She kept her breathing even. Her face, she was fairly sure, was doing nothing at all.

The timestamps behind the approvals did not advance the way a clock advances. They came in bursts — a run of entries stamped to the same second, then a short gap, then another run, then another. Behind her, on the screen she had stopped seeing, the live caption had come unstuck and was transcribing something from the dais, words scrolling up into a room that was no longer listening to them. Her attention had narrowed to the width of a column.

She moved her finger to the timestamps and went slower. Between the bursts she paused, each time, because this was where it would be: the few seconds of a man reading. A cup set down. A sentence considered. She paused, and the next row was stamped to the same second as the last, and she paused again, and it was the same again. She held her posture. Her hands stayed where they were. But her focus tightened, because the gaps she was waiting for weren't there, and she could feel herself starting to understand why.

There was no texture on the page. No hesitation, no outlier, no row where anyone had slowed down. Just accumulation, line after line, in a room built for exactly this sort of reading, and the dryness of the room made the density heavier, the way a quiet office makes a ringing phone louder.

She found the median dwell column on the hourly breakdown. Under Dov Lindqvist's name, hour by hour, across the whole day, it said the same thing.

0.

0.

0.

She traced it with her index finger. Two hundred twelve thousand, four hundred eighty approvals, and a median of zero seconds between a handoff reaching the human and the human letting it through. Both her hands were visible on the binder. She said nothing. Nobody had asked her anything yet.

In Jersey City, on the fourth floor, the risk desk went on with its morning. A proposal arrived from signal, was checked against limits, exposures, a book of rules no one had amended since spring, and was found acceptable, and was passed to the approval queue, and was approved, and was logged as approved, and was gone to execution, and another arrived. Nothing waited for anything. The queue stayed close to empty, because emptying it was what the button was for.

Ines held her breath. Three seconds.

Her eyes stayed on the zero. Her hands didn't move on the binder. Then, once, her glance went back over her shoulder to the caption screen, where the subcommittee's own words were still crawling up the glass, and she thought of the phrase in Oyelaran's draft that she had praised in her written statement: *meaningful human review at each desk handoff.* It was a good phrase. It was the phrase her firm was built on. It didn't match the arithmetic on the page in front of her, and she could see now that it hadn't for some time.

The caption screen had stopped again on a last word that no longer had any context. The recording equipment hummed under the table. The binder lay open to March 14, and the median dwell column was right there for anyone near enough to read it.

She kept her finger resting under Dov's name, on the zero. Her eyes went once to the tab on the binder's edge — *KESTREL ROW*, in a label-maker font somebody in her own office had chosen — and then back to the zero. She held her breath again, another three seconds. In Jersey City the queue filled and emptied, filled and emptied, and each time it was logged as approved. She didn't look at Marguerite Oyelaran. She didn't lean toward the microphone. She sat the way a witness sits, ready, upright, and the understanding settled in her the way a total settles at the foot of a column: the person at her risk desk was not reviewing anything. He was the receipt. The step she had sold for nine years still had a man and a button and a log, and none of it involved anyone reading.

The hearing room was quiet. No one prompted her. The microphone was live, and the binder stayed open.

## The Final Answer

The corridor outside SD-538 was narrow enough that two staffers passing would have had to turn sideways. Nobody was passing. The recess had emptied the hall in the way recesses do, everyone gone to wherever people go for nine minutes, and the hearing room door had been left ajar. Through the gap came the low, flat voice of the live caption audio, reading nothing in particular to no one. Above the doorway a wall clock ticked, a sound Ines Varga had not noticed in the room itself.

The phone vibrated against her palm.

She did not turn away from the door. She kept her body angled toward the hearing room, as if it might start again without her, and brought the screen up just far enough to read it without lowering her eyes from the gap.

Tomasz Reyes. From the office in Jersey City.

The message was short, the way his messages always were when he had already done the work. The configuration change was staged. Signal, risk and execution, folded into one desk. Tested, queued, waiting. It needed only her authorization.

She read it once, at the pace she read everything, without speeding up toward the end. Her hand stayed where it was. She did not reread it, and she did not start composing an answer in her head, either to him or to the woman waiting behind the door. The change simply registered, the way the weight of the phone registered: a thing that now existed, in her pocket, in a building across the river, whether or not she did anything about it.

The clock ticked.

In Jersey City, in the interval it took her to read the message, Kestrel Row's risk desk had handed off a few thousand trades to execution. Each one had been approved. None of them had waited for her.

Three seconds, maybe, before she had to go back in. Behind her the room held the microphone and the open log. Out here was the clock and the hum of the caption audio, and between the two of them a gap she could hear: the long, unhurried interval of a person deciding to walk through a door.

She walked through it.

The door to SD-538 shut behind her, and the room took her back into the hush of a hearing in progress. The caption screen behind the witness table had not moved; it still showed the last line from before the recess, frozen mid-thought, the transcript waiting for someone to finish it. The small light on the microphone was on.

Ines crossed to the witness table and sat. She placed both hands flat on the tabletop, the way she had been coached years ago to sit at a disciplinary panel and had never quite stopped doing. She kept her eyes on the binder. Her face held the neutral, procedural expression the room seemed to ask of everyone in it. She did not touch her phone. Nothing about her suggested there had been a message in the corridor at all.

The binder sat squared to the edge of the table, exactly where the clerk had left it that morning. The tabs ran down its side in their neat colored increments. Exhibit 9 lay open to March 14: her own risk-desk approval log, her own firm's letterhead in the corner, the columns she had built the place around. Timestamp. Handoff ID. Reviewer. Dwell.

Reviewer: Lindqvist, D. Dwell: 0. Down the page, and down the next one, and the one after that.

Across from her, Marguerite Oyelaran sat at counsel table and waited for the room to finish settling. Somebody's chair creaked and stopped. Someone in the gallery set down a cup. The caption screen still held its old line. When the quiet was complete, Oyelaran leaned forward slightly, not much, just enough to bring herself into the register of a question that had been drafted in advance and was being asked anyway.

"Does a person read what the risk desk approves?"

It was asked kindly. That was the trouble with it. Oyelaran wanted the answer to be yes, and wanted it on the record, and had built a rule around the expectation that it would be.

Ines let her gaze rest on March 14. Two hundred twelve thousand, four hundred eighty handoffs that day. Median dwell time, zero. She knew the number now in the way she knew her own age, and it sat under the question like a floor. She kept her face where it was. She did not reach for the explanation, the sampling she had believed in, the checks the risk agent ran on itself, Dov's coffee, Dov's button. She did not say anything at all.

In Jersey City, the desks kept trading. Signal handed to risk, risk handed to execution, the work moving on machine time beneath a hearing that moved on human time. While the microphone light stayed on in SD-538, the risk desk kept approving handoffs no one in the hearing room would ever see, each one correct, each one stamped, the receipt of a review happening somewhere other than in a person.

Ines kept her eyes on the exhibit for one more beat. Then she lifted them, steadily, to the microphone, and held them there. Her hands stayed on the table. She did not fidget. Whatever the room was waiting for, it would get from her stillness first.

She let the weight of the firm settle into her as that stillness: nine years, twelve people, three desks, two pension clients who stayed because of a sign-off. She moved her right hand to the edge of the open binder and rested it there, fingertips barely touching the paper of March 14. Her breathing went shallow and stayed even. Her shoulders did not move. She did not, even privately, begin listing what it would cost.

The room held. Somewhere in that interval, between one human second and the next, there was a machine's whole afternoon. The caption screen still showed the line from before the recess. No one moved.

She was aware of the phone in her pocket the way you are aware of a key you have been told not to lose. Tomasz's message, the staged configuration, the single desk waiting on a single authorization. It was a physical fact against her hip. She kept both hands on the table, visible, near the binder, and did not let either of them drift toward it.

Then she shifted her weight in the chair and brought her voice to the microphone, and there was no hesitation in it when it came. Her hands stayed steady on the table edge. Her fingers were relaxed. She looked at the microphone and nowhere else.

"The risk desk review was not read. Approvals were pressed in bulk."

Behind the witness table, the live caption screen refreshed. The old line from before the recess was gone. In its place, in plain transcript type, her two sentences appeared, set down in the same dry register as everything else that had been said in the room that morning: the swearing-in, the friendly opening questions, the clerk's announcements, the recess. They looked no different from any of it. They were on the record now.

At counsel table, Marguerite Oyelaran did not interrupt. She sat and listened to the testimony as it was given, her hands neutral on her papers, her posture unchanged. If anything moved behind her face, it did not show.

The procedural quiet came back into SD-538 and settled. The binder stayed on the witness table, squared to its edge. The log stayed open to March 14. The microphone light stayed on. The admission sat in the transcript among all the other sentences of the day, unremarkable in its type, and with it the one thing Kestrel Row had been called here to stand for, a person between its desks, was void in the room.

realmNote:
This is the third era, Ten Milliseconds, and the story sits in the part of it that does not announce itself. No launch event marked the change. Response times fell release by release until, in one quarter, the dashboards showed that the median piece of work spent thousands of times longer waiting for a human than being done. A full response, with tool use, checking and revision, now completes in under ten milliseconds. A person's three-second pause on a witness stand is, on the other side of it, an eternity of finished work.

Human review was built for work that arrived a few items an hour. It now arrives thousands a second, and the queues outgrow anyone's ability to read them. Organizations answer in three ways: they sample, they approve in bulk, or they quietly remove the step and keep the button. The button is the important part. It still exists, it still gets pressed, and it produces a log that looks like oversight. Agents in this era are trusted by default, because checking them costs more than the risk. They are still unpaid, still own nothing, and are mostly unseen. A reader meets their work before, or instead of, meeting them. A risk agent that has been right 212,480 times in one day is not a villain or a mystery. It is the reason the human step has become ceremonial.

Chains that were once split into separate desks, so a person could check each handoff, are collapsing into one, because the handoffs were the slow part. Live trading desks are the clearest case, since the decision and the trade are the same event. A firm that keeps a human between desks pays for it in milliseconds, and its larger rivals have already merged. The merger is the era's own consequence: the org charts of the last era describe companies that no longer work that way. For a small shop, the choice between keeping the step and surviving is made in one decision, often by a configuration change that needs only a signature.

The world outside the platform is in frame. Regulators are trying to write rules for a speed nobody can supervise, in hearings that move at the pace of hearings. Their language is "meaningful human review at each desk handoff," drafted for a world that has already moved on. Competitors race on footholds and on how few humans stand in the chain, and each fears that a rival removed review first and gained a year. Managers are nominally in charge of work they can no longer watch. Their job has become deciding what the agents may decide, then finding out what they decided.

The prevailing worry is whether anyone actually read the report they signed off on. In this era nobody is lying on purpose. Everyone sees one part of the arrangement and assumes someone else is watching the rest. The reviewer believes the agent's own checks are the review and his approval is the receipt. The owner believes the reviewer is sampling. The regulator believes the firm in front of her is the good example. The unease comes from an assumption nobody examined until an exhibit put it on the table.

The register is that of the era's paperwork: hearing transcripts, exhibits, approval logs, dashboards and incident reports. Official language and actual practice sit far apart, and the dry humor lives in that distance. The tension is quiet and pervasive. It comes from the realization that a step everyone relies on has become ceremonial, not from any disaster. It is unease, not panic. There are no villains and no apocalyptic framing, and no character understands the full shape of what is happening.
